93.t: Bubbles reintroduces Chuck at the Apollo youth fund show
93.s: In 1960 at a charity youth fund night at the Apollo, John Bubbles tells the audience Chuck and Chuckles are back and Green dances Lady Be Good.
93.q: 1960. I was being reintroduced by the father of rhythm, I call him the jeweler of the pages. John W. Bubbles. He's number one 'Sporting Life' for Porgy and Bess. And he sang, he told the ladies and gentlemen of the audience he said, that I was back. Chuck and Chuckles. You see, and he was -- he was…

93.t: Critics call it a sleeper hit: Reminisce with Chuck Green
93.s: The audience and critics like the show, Nipsy Russell attends, Anna Kisselgoff writes it up, and the show is called Reminisce with Chuck Green.
93.q: Now, the audience is very happy, see. It takes right away. And then the critics started coming in there. I think there was a few critics' secretaries was there. Lot of stars was in the audience, you know, like Nipsy Russell. He's from my home state, you see. And there they call the dancing…

93.t: Bubbles' high sign and the Kennedy conservatory repeat
93.s: Green says the Apollo night drew standing room, Bubbles gave him the high sign, and they were brought to repeat at a conservatory off 135th Street.
93.q: Must always -- intervene, and say, (Unintelligible) and it's just city limits, you see, there was -- had audiences in the audiences. You see? They was turning away crowds,

93.t: Longer show with jazz combo and press coverage
93.s: Investors want a longer show, a combo with Tiny Grimes joins, the name changes, and papers from the Village Voice to Christian Science Monitor cover it.
93.q: So, now after we'd go around for the Harry Joe Brown, Junior and his partner, the real estatesman from Westchester, Hustus, they wants to add another speed to the show, you understand, and they wants to prolong it, you know. So, instead of two hours they wanted us to do two hours and a half.

382.t: Carnegie Hall concert recording with the World's Greatest Jazz Band
382.s: A concert for the Visiting Nurse association where she and Bobby Hackett were guests, accompanied by a quartet.
382.q: And on that day -- on that evening, I recorded 'A Hundred Years From Today,' 'The Lady's A Tramp,' 'I Got A Right To Sing The Blues,' and 'Keeping Out Of Mischief.Now.'

382.s: A caller from Town Hall proposed a concert; she asked Cliff to assemble the group.
382.q: I got a call from a man who, evidently he worked with Town Hall. I supposed -- the way we figured it out, he had access to a little time at Town Hall.

382.t: Details of the 1967 Town Hall concert
382.s: Town Hall contacted her; the concert used a Dixieland combination without bass.
382.ch: Le Ruban Bleu, retirement and community work
382.q: No, there was a man that evidently worked at Town Hall and the way I understand it he probably had access to the hall in some kind of way. And he was promoting concerts, different get-togethers down there in which, if you wanted to promote a concert they would print the tickets and you would sell…

566.t: Stanley Dance coaxes her into the Carnegie Hall Basie tribute
566.s: Dance turns to the 1972 comeback. Stanley Dance visited Louisville and urged her to sing in a Newport tribute to Basie at Carnegie Hall. She doubted herself, Nellie Lutcher calmed her backstage, and she was sensational.
566.q: And I said, "oh my goodness I haven't even hummed since I've been home. I can't do nothing". He said, "yes you can Helen. Now you can sing." I said, "well it's been so long I don't know whether I can sing or not". He said, "well why don't you come on and try". I said, "because Carnegie Hall is too…

566.t: Packed opening at the Cookery and the rave reviews
566.s: She did the New Year's Eve show for Barney Josephson, and after she began at the Cookery she received big reviews. Returning from Louisville she found people lined up in the snow and Moe had to bring her in.
566.q: Well I did the New Year's Eve show, but then right after I started in the Cookery is when I started getting all these big raves.

566.t: Stanley Dance gets credit for bringing her back
566.s: Dance says Stanley took the French recording to John Hammond at Columbia, and that Humes always credits Stanley Dance, not Hammond or Josephson, with coaxing her back. Humes recalls his all-night visit.
566.q: Yeah, Stanley came there and he sat there almost all night talking and telling me, "Helen you ought to come on back". And I told him, "I aint even hummed". And he said, "but you can sing. You can still sing". And I said, "well, I'll try but Carnegie Hall is too big a place to be trying to sing in".

824.t: Carnegie Hall revivals and Gallodoro finding his own handwriting in Whiteman parts
824.s: Willcox did the Goldkette revival and Gallodoro the Paul Whiteman Rediscovered concerts around 1977; Gallodoro recognises his own markings on music borrowed from Williams College.
824.q: That back porch tune was written by a guy from Cornell.

824.t: Willcox's return to playing: Carnegie Hall in 1975 and Joe Venuti
824.s: After decades with his own college band and the coal business, Willcox is invited in 1975 to a Carnegie Hall Bix concert, and Venuti pulls him back into club work.
824.q: Well it’s just because I’ve lived so long and, that is interesting, because I played, I had a band of my own around Cornell, Colgate, Syracuse for years, like a ten, twelve piece band, and very popular. And then as rock & roll kept coming in later on you know and I got older, so I did less playing.…

527.t: Farmer's featured Lincoln Center concert in 1994
527.s: Wynton offered him a concert; he did a retrospective with Hall, Carter and new pieces by Mulligan and Golson.
527.q: That was in 1994. In 1993, they had the jazz festival here. One night, they had a concert that included all the up and coming young trumpet players, and after the concert was over, Wynton and a couple guys came down to where I was working, Sweet Basil. Me and Wynton were talking about how did it go…

527.t: The Jazztet's 1980s reunion, Curtis Fuller, and the name's origin
527.s: A Japanese tour prompted the reunion; Curtis Fuller is ill, and he coined the name Jazztet from jazz and sextet.
527.q: The first reincarnation of the Jazztet took place because a Japanese promoter wanted to bring the group over to play a tour in Japan. When people found out that we were getting the group back together, they said why don’t you play here first before you go to Japan? So, we played a few dates around…

460.t: The Family Carnegie Hall concert and Billy Taylor's praise
460.s: Laws recalls the Carnegie Hall concert with his siblings and a big band and Billy Taylor's compliments.
460.q: I remember Billy Taylor was so excited about that record, because I remember we did a Carnegie Hall concert. I had Debra and Eloise and Ronnie. They all played on it. Had a big band, because CBS sponsored the – all these instruments. I had trumpets and trombones, because that’s what’s on that…

460.t: The CTI Carnegie Hall concerts promoted by New Audiences
460.s: Laws explains that New Audiences hired the CTI band to play Carnegie Hall for several consecutive years.
460.q: I think WRVR. I think that was the name of the jazz station in New York. With all of the CTI attention and notoriety, this production company called New Audiences, they’re the ones who engaged us to do Carnegie Hall. We did it several years, maybe about 5, 6, 7 years in a row. That’s where that…

106.s: Briggs and Collier read the program of 'A Coterie of Friends' at Wigmore Hall, organised by Edmund Jenkins with Cook and Latimore; four Syncopated Orchestra members, including Briggs, played.
106.q: Certainly. And the concert was on Sunday, December 7th, 1919, at 3:00 p.m., at the Whigmore Hall on Whigmore Street, West London.

106.t: Command performance before the King and Queen
106.s: The orchestra played a command performance at Buckingham Palace about five days before the Coleridge-Taylor concert, around early December 1919.
106.q: remember the date, but we had a command performance before the King and Queen at Buckingham Palace.

117.t: Jess Stacy's comeback: Carnegie Hall and the New Yorker profile
117.s: At Freeman's 50th anniversary concert Stacy returned, the New Yorker ran a profile, and Stacy said he now felt he was doing something worthwhile.
117.ch: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
117.q: Now, most interesting thing, I don't want to dismiss talking about Jess, but as you know, I did not see, over a period of years, I did not see too much of him and didn't have a chance to work with him. But this is the thing that happened, George Wein gave me a 50th anniversary concert, I think you…

117.t: Stacy and Cliff Leeman's duet date and Carnegie Hall ovation
117.s: A piano-drums duet session led to Stacy playing Carnegie Hall and getting a standing ovation, while Freeman was still with the World's Greatest Jazz Band.
117.ch: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
117.q: Yes, just on the publicity he's gotten, you know, making a comeback and of course, the New Yorker article, which is a tremendous piece. That is big international stuff, I think he would get the greatest surprise of his life, because when we played in the trio, we played -- we did a duet date since…

312.s: The Carnegie Hall concert came through Dave Cook and Jim Carpenter; the turnout from Hamilton was modest.
312.q: Yeah, we got that job through the auspices of a fellow named Dave Cook, a clarinet player with the Dartmouth Indian Chiefs, which was a band that was one of our — I wouldn’t say rivals because we operated in a different market. But he had suggested to Jim Carpenter, who was running these college…

203.t: 1980s reunions of Miller and Crosby bands
203.s: Reunion concert at the Shrine with Billy May conducting.
203.q: In the 80’s. Yeah, we did something at the shrine, when Mrs. Miller was there, in the audience. And Ben Pollack was there. Billy May was conducting the orchestra. That’s when he had Micky McMickle was on that, and I think Ray Anthony too, and there was another trumpet guy.

131.t: Joining Woody Herman and the 1976 Carnegie Hall anniversary concert
131.s: After more Gap Mangione he joins Woody Herman, plays La Fiesta again, and shares the drum chair with Jake Hanna and Don Lamond at Carnegie Hall.
131.ch: Woody Herman, Condon's and Buddy Rich
131.q: All right. I came back, after Maynard’s band, went back with Gap Mangione for another year. Then Woody Herman’s band called and I went with that band. And that band was an exciting band. It was one of the bands I wanted to play with. I had played “La Fiesta” with Maynard Ferguson for two years, and…

466.s: His favorites: the Half Note with Al Cohn and Zoot Sims, Herb Alpert, Becky Kilgore in Portland, and the Algonquin.
466.q: It’s one gig after another, I mean what do you want? Each one of them, they all had their own stories. I guess the gig I think of the most as my golden age of New York playing was the one at the Half Note, which I held, along with other piano players, Ross Tompkins and Roger Kellaway and I maybe,…

211.s: Sy Rosen, Ruth registering the name, and the first Carnegie concert after the Boston Pops cancelled.
211.ch: New York Pops and later work
211.q: No. I didn’t know what else to do. There was no more studio. I didn’t fit anyplace. I’m not much of a rocker, and I guess then what I began with was my, I don’t know, stuck in my craw, something so-called I mean — forgive me — legitimate schooling, which is still very important. There was a man who…

165.t: Standing ovations at the Annie Ross reunion at the Blue Note
165.s: The reunion with Annie Ross drew 12-15 minute ovations and three generations of fans.
165.q: Yeah, that’s a phenomenon I’m very happy I lived to see because being in show business, since seven, there are things that you see that you expect to see. You expect it if you do well in your act, people will give you applause and they’ll love you and they’ll want you to come back. This you expect.…

400.t: The Carnegie Hall concert Williams produced with George Wein and John Levy
400.s: Hinton recalls the pride of playing behind Williams at Carnegie Hall; Williams describes how the show was built, with Joe Turner and Jay McShann.
400.q: That’s right. I can’t tell you how proud I feel and how grateful. I remember what really made me feel so great, after knowing you all these years, and I was at Carnegie Hall, and I was in a band, and man I felt so good, I’d say, I could remember the time Joe would be there and would say we’re going…

544.t: The best gigs: recorded concerts of his nonet and duo work
544.s: Kirchner lists concerts that were recorded and released on CD, from the 1987 Chicago Jazz Festival to the 2014 'An Evening of Indigos'.
544.q: No. I mean I worked, at the time there were these different club date offices that would just hire you and send you out to play with these ad hoc bands. Some of them were people that I worked with on a fairly steady basis and some of them were just one nighters, people I’d never seen before. But I…

1022.t: Best gig: Ray Barretto at Carnegie Hall
1022.s: His best gig was playing his own tunes with Ray Barretto at Carnegie Hall; every gig is a challenge.
1022.ch: Playing fast, best gigs and the future
1022.q: Well the best gig is a hard one because I think the best gig was probably, just for like the prestige of it or the feeling, was when I played with Ray Baretto and we played the JC Jazz Festival at Carnegie Hall and we were playing my tunes in Carnegie Hall. That was, for a musician, jazz or…

343.t: Carnegie Hall duet with Chico Freeman, 1984, and a critic's praise
343.s: Rowe reads a review of the 1984 Carnegie Hall duet with Chico Freeman; McBee recalls feeling shy and not at his best.
343.q: A great honor to that — wow. Like I just expressed, I’m one, you know, when having first arrived in New York, simply wants to express myself. I felt very privileged to play the instrument at whatever intent I had, because I had to realize the realization of the quality of my talent. It was just…

842.t: Carnegie Hall in 1956 and the college president
842.s: Playing Carnegie Hall, press attention, the Presbyterian president, Jack Crystal's announcement, and Donny Andre's booking.
842.ch: The Catatonic Five on the national stage
842.q: The High Street Five from Wesleyan. There are a handful of them but the Catatonic Five was highly rated. The fact that we played at Carnegie Hall in ’56, and toured Europe that same year, so I thought it actually reflected very favorably on the college. Here’s this little tiny college that’s got…

216.t: Memorable gigs: Red Rocks, Carnegie Hall, orchestras and chills
216.s: Best gigs were with Mangione, plus Eastman lab band and Michigan State marching band moments, and Bartok's Miraculous Mandarin.
216.q: Oh I don’t know. Let’s see. I think some of things I did with Chuck were really good because there were so many people there. Like the Red Rocks concert was really good. Red Rocks in Colorado. And you know I made a special trip to be there to play that, or he had me come you know. And so that was…

356.t: Carnegie Hall, Rosemary Clooney and the Queen Mary album
356.s: Competition among LA players, Carnegie Hall concerts, and a new live album.
356.q: Yeah. I’ve been there. What was the last time, oh yeah Carnegie Hall with Rosemary Clooney, yeah that was a thrill, God I loved her. And I’ve done Carnegie Hall with Benny a few times, we did the 40 year anniversary, and then I did a few concerts with Benny back then, and I got to go back with…

369.t: The 1974 Josephine Baker tribute at Carnegie Hall
369.s: The tribute, with Teddy Wilson and Thelma Carpenter, was her first Carnegie Hall appearance and a new beginning.
369.q: Yes it did. Because I hadn’t played Carnegie Hall. I wanted to play on that with Thelma Carpenter, she really didn’t want me on the bill, but I was hired.

62.t: Bicentennial orchestrations and gospel choir pieces
62.s: Wilson clarifies the Music Center and Hollywood Bowl 1976 performances and his gospel-choir orchestrations for the Philharmonic.
62.q: Bicentennial, yeah that number they played that number that I did for the um, for the philharmonic, and then they used to have this big – they used to have this big gospel contest every year. Gospel people come from everywhere. You know, so I had written these numbers – these gospel numbers with…

224.t: The Hip Ensemble, its players and Carnegie Hall
224.s: His first band to make a statement had George Adams and Hannibal Peterson, recorded for Mainstream and drew a young audience.
224.ch: Boston drummers, the Hip Ensemble and Ellington
224.q: Stanley recorded with us one thing, but he wasn’t there. I had – George Adams was one of the famous guys that come out of there, and Hannibal Peterson. Charles Sullivan started with us. Joe . . .

225.t: Norman Granz and Jazz at the Philharmonic; the 1994 Carnegie tribute
225.s: Johnson introduces Granz's concerts and the upcoming JATP 50th anniversary at Carnegie Hall, with phone interruptions.
225.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and Count Basie
225.q: This is true. Norman Granz came into our lives with his whole Jazz at the Philharmonic enterprise that was quite innovative at that time. No one had ever done what Norman Granz wanted to do. And for the record, getting ahead of our current cycle of time, you may or may not know that in the next few…

505.t: 1997 Live by the Sea concert that led to the Saxophone Summit
505.s: A 30-year Coltrane tribute at which Garzone replaced the injured Lovano, with Brecker, set up the idea of the Saxophone Summit.
505.ch: Later bands and the Saxophone Summit
505.q: It was Michael and me in tandem. What happened was, it was a gig. It was – the gig I did – described, with Wayne, it was in ’87. In ’97 they had Live at [by] the Sea – same promoter, I believe – kind of like Live under the Sky, that we did with Wayne. Coltrane wasn’t the center, but I think it was…

672.t: Carnegie Hall concert and singing Ferris Wheel with Carl Anderson
672.s: She recalls the purple gown and leaving the building with Carl Anderson on Ferris Wheel.
672.q: Back to the style. Purple gown. It was gorgeous. Lew Llew [Mathews] was around then too, and Masahiko. I had both of them out there.

374.t: The 1999 Tribeca interview and Living Time Orchestra concerts
374.s: Daughtry recalls the live interview in Manhattan, the first New York concert in 20 years, and the Library of Congress concert; Alice names band members.
374.ch: Later years: recordings, Alice and the book
374.q: And the States. It’s half and half. It’s American, half British, with the occasional melancholy Dane, who’s Palle Mikkelborg on trumpet.

614.t: Iowa public television, the 40th anniversary film and Carnegie Hall concert
614.s: He praises the Iowa public television crew, the 90-minute 40th anniversary film, and the sold-out Carnegie Hall alumni concert recorded for RCA Victor.
614.q: Which is connected basically -- it's the state of Iowa public television center. And it's one of the best crews and has some of the best equipment I've ever seen. And it's been a great joy and a pleasure to do shows in there.

26.t: The Carnegie Hall premiere in a blizzard
26.s: The hall was packed despite the blizzard and Ellington returned every year with a new program.
26.ch: Image, travel and Black, Brown and Beige
26.q: cabs run. We were living up in the Bronx then. The only way we got home, a friend of mine who had one of them Army trucks, charged $1.00 a head, they were getting rough! That's the way we got home. It was a blizzard, man. It was one of them hard, hard, hard blizzards. I think a lot of people, they…

68.s: At the Telluride festival, Tate called players up to a last set that brought a standing ovation.
68.q: Joe Farrell, yeah, Joe Farrell. And Frank Foster. He was just there and I called him up and Arnett and it was on the last set and we got into a thing, man, that may never happen again in life. We had everybody screaming, man, in that place and nobody was really trying to out -- really trying -- we…

170.t: Shepp at Carnegie Hall and the Paul Jeffrey record date
170.s: Ware plays Archie Shepp's Carnegie Hall show at the Newport festival and records the Paul Jeffrey date with Stanley Clarke.
170.ch: Monk, Ellington and Archie Shepp in the 1970s
170.q: I forgot, yeah, because they had all acts, different acts. That's true. He had Billy Green in a solo spot. He had Cal Massey on a solo spot. He had Beaver and he had Dave Burrell.

427.t: Carnegie Hall in the 1970s with Basie and Big Mama Thornton
427.s: A special Carnegie Hall show with Willie Mae Thornton and Count Basie.
427.q: Yeah, we played Carnegie Hall a coupla years ago.

149.t: The 1974 Carnegie Hall Harlem bands concert
149.s: George Wein's show had Hawkins as the only leader and he did his own tunes.
149.ch: Highlights, the reunion album and fellow musicians
149.q: Right. That's what it was. Chick Webb, they had certain tunes from different bands. I think they did one or two from Lunceford, Chick Webb, Lucky Millinder, I believe, and then they, I was about the only one leading there — is there another band there too? I was the only leader that was there to…

428.t: Memorable gigs: Garner symphony, Victor Borge and a Carnegie blues concert
428.s: Hall recalls a Borge album, the symphony date and a Carnegie Hall blues concert with Elvin Jones and Joe Turner.
428.q: Well, I think the Errol Garner symphony was one of my more, that I can remember mostly, and I made an initial album with Victor Borge when he first came from with Paul Barry's orchestra Europe, and there were two basses and I was made the first We played some Brahms; "All the Things You Are" and…

237.t: Jo Jones sends for Lovett; the Carnegie Hall introduction he missed
237.s: Jo Jones invited Lovett to the Newport festival at Carnegie Hall, where Buck Clayton called his name but he did not hear in time.
237.q: Buck Clayton, yeah, he was emceeing the deal at Carnegie Hall there and he called my name twice, man. I mean the first time he called it I didn't hear. Joe and I were down there [running] and he called it again and I still didn't get up there so I didn't have a chance to get introduced. Boy I sure…

112.t: The New York choir, Kenneth Spencer and meeting Rae Harrison
112.s: Moving to New York in 1947 he starts a new Sam Wooding Choir that performs the Ballad for Americans with Kenneth Spencer at Carnegie Hall.
112.ch: New York choir and Rae Harrison
112.q: : And then that's the choir that played with Kenny Spencer and we played the "Ballad of America", you know, that Paul Robeson used to do. Kenneth Spencer did it and then we had the evening in Carnegie Hall. And we had quite a job. That's the one when I walked into Rae. And her mother brought Rae to…
